query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloys, the nature of the substituent element X governs the formation of a protective oxide layer during exposure to high-temperature oxidative or corrosive environments. Specifically, when X promotes slow cation diffusion and good lattice matching (as in the cases of Al or Si), a coherent, thin, and slowly thickening oxide scale forms and remains adherent above 900 °C. In contrast, if X does not promote these conditions (as with Mn), the resulting oxide is thicker, less uniform, and prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, single‐phase CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloy with X = Al, Si, or Mn.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for prolonged durations.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (≥900 °C) exposure under a controlled oxidizing or corrosive environment with defined oxygen partial pressure or aggressive species concentration.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a coherent, continuous protective oxide scale (preferably α‐Al2O3 or SiO2 for Al or Si containing alloys) at the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation modulated by the choice of X: when X (Al or Si) slows cation diffusion and minimizes lattice mismatch at the oxide/metal interface, it leads to a slow-growing, adherent oxide layer; when X (Mn) does not provide these benefits, rapid oxide growth with high defect density results in cracking and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys incorporating Al or Si are expected to develop a thin, uniform, and slowly growing protective oxide scale with minimal cracking, whereas the Mn-containing alloy will form a thicker, nonuniform oxide that undergoes cracking and spallation under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: The CrFeCoNiMn alloy serves as the baseline where the oxide layer is expected to be unstable and prone to spallation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to equiatomic, single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloys exposed to high-temperature (above 900 °C) oxidative or corrosive environments; different microstructures (e.g., multiphase alloys) or lower temperatures may exhibit different oxide behaviors.
generation.uncertainty: While the general trends are expected, the exact influence of microstructural variations and exposure duration on oxide coherence and growth kinetics remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of equiatomic, single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloys with X substituted by Al, Si, and Mn under identical processing conditions. Expose each sample to a controlled oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for selected durations. Follow the evolution of the oxide scales using surface characterization techniques.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and uniformity (via cross-sectional microscopy and weight gain measurements)
Crack density and spallation events (via SEM analysis)
Phase composition of the oxides (via XRD and EDS mapping)
Growth kinetics of the oxide scale over time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with X = Al or Si do not form a significantly more coherent, thin, and slow-growing oxide scale compared to the Mn-containing alloy, or if the Mn alloy exhibits oxide scale stability comparable to the Al/Si variants, then the hypothesis that the nature of X governs the protective oxide layer formation is falsified.

Various stability criteria developed for high-entropy alloys are applied to compositions produced by mechanical alloying. While they agree with the annealed samples, these criteria fail to describe the as-milled metastable systems, highlighting the ability of mechanical alloying to overcome the limitations imposed by these criteria. The criteria are based on atomic size (Ω ≥ 1.1 and δr ≤ 6.6%) and/or electronegativity misfit, as well as on mixing enthalpy (Λ>0.95 J mol−1K−1 and −5 kJ mol−1<∆Hmix<0), or purely thermodynamic (ϕYe>20; ϕKing>1; Teff<500 K). These criteria are applied to several compositions found in the literature and to two metastable fcc solid solutions produced by mechanical alloying with compositions Al0.75CoXFeNi with X = Cr and Mn. Single-phase microstructures are stable up to above 600 K, leading to more stable multiphase systems after annealing above this temperature. Mössbauer spectrometry shows that, whereas the alloy with Cr is paramagnetic in the as-milled and annealed state, the alloy with Mn changes from paramagnetic to ferromagnetic behavior (Curie temperature ~700 K) after annealing. Cr’s outward diffusion is faster than oxygen’s inward diffusion, so chromia scales usually grow outward, consisting of fractions of iron, nickel, and manganese. However, at temperatures above 900 °C, chromia can form volatile CrO3. Aluminum, another effective alloying element, forms a protective Al2O3 layer, offering significant resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion. Al2O3 scales grow slower than chromium oxide scales and are more stable, especially against aggressive carbon or sulfur species. However, the formation of alumina and consequent depletion of Al in the alloy could result in structural instability in the alloy. The formation of oxide scales in HEAs containing multiple oxide-forming species is influenced by their intricate chemistries and microstructures. High-temperature, long-duration oxidation studies on bulk alloys typically reveal dominant oxide films composed of complex ternary and quaternary oxides. The polycrystalline nature of these alloys, combined with surface heterogeneity and phase instabilities at high temperatures, leads to highly variable oxide structures. drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, a stable and coherent, slow‐growing protective oxide layer will form and persist above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere if the alloying element X promotes the selective oxidation of elements (e.g., Cr, Al, or Si) that yield an adherent oxide scale with minimal lattice mismatch. In contrast, if X (such as Mn) does not favor formation of such a scale, the oxide layer will be unstable and prone to cracking or spalling.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equiatomic single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloy with X chosen as either Al, Si, or Mn.
drafts.intervention: Exposure of the alloy to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for extended durations.
drafts.conditions: High-temperature exposure (>900 °C) in a controlled oxidative environment (with defined oxygen partial pressure) simulating service conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: The presence and continuity of a slow-growing, coherent oxide scale (e.g., Cr-rich, Al2O3, or SiO2 based) at the alloy surface.
drafts.mechanism: Selective oxidation: In compositions where X promotes the formation of a high-melting, slow-growing, low-strain oxide (via appropriate diffusion and low lattice misfit with the substrate), the oxide scale remains adherent. In alloys with X (like Mn) that do not enhance such selective oxidation, rapid oxide growth and the development of high defect densities lead to cracking and spallation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys where X is Al or Si will display a continuous, slowly thickening, coherent oxide scale with minimal cracking, whereas alloys with X = Mn will show rapid oxide growth accompanied by cracks and spallation.
drafts.baseline: The CrFeCoNiMn alloy composition serves as a control where the oxide layer is expected to be unstable.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloys under service conditions above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres; results may differ outside these temperature or environmental boundaries.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare single-phase equiatomic CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Al, Si, and Mn. Expose each alloy to a controlled atmosphere with a fixed partial pressure of oxygen at temperatures above 900 °C for various durations. Use standardized surface characterization techniques to monitor oxide layer thickness, microstructure, and occurrence of cracks or spallation.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness over time (e.g., via cross-sectional microscopy)
Crack density and spallation events using scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Phase identification of oxide constituents using X-ray diffraction (XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with X = Al or Si do not form a coherent, slow-growing oxide layer (i.e., if they display similar cracking/spallation behavior and rapid oxide growth as the X = Mn alloy), or if the oxide layer in the X = Mn alloy shows similar stability, then the hypothesis that selective oxidation mediated by the choice of X governs the stability of the oxide layer is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the choice of substituent element (X) determines the protective oxide layer's stability above 900 °C by influencing the cation diffusion kinetics and oxide crystal structure. Specifically, when X is Si or Al, slower cation diffusion and a better lattice match at the oxide/metal interface promote the formation of a coherent, slow-growing, adherent oxide layer, whereas when X is Mn, faster cation diffusion and defect-prone oxide growth result in a brittle, non-coherent scale that cracks and spalls.
drafts.material_initial_state: Single-phase metallic solid-solution state of CrFeCoNiX alloys at room temperature.
drafts.intervention: Exposure of the alloys to temperatures above 900 °C under a defined oxidative or corrosive atmosphere.
drafts.conditions: Controlled high-temperature exposures (above 900 °C), in a standardized oxidative or corrosive environment, with careful monitoring of thermal cycles to observe oxide scale formation and integrity over time.
drafts.structural_mediator: The mismatch strain and diffusion barrier properties at the oxide/metal interface mediated by the substitute element in the alloy.
drafts.mechanism: Element-specific alloying alters cation diffusion kinetics and the resultant oxide crystal structure. Si and Al slow down cation diffusion and reduce mismatch strain at the oxide/metal boundary, aiding the development of a coherent, adherent oxide. In contrast, Mn increases cation mobility and defect density, causing rapid oxide growth that is structurally unstable and prone to cracking/spallation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys with Si or Al as the X component will form a slow-growing, coherent, and adherent oxide layer that persists during prolonged exposure above 900 °C, whereas alloys with Mn will develop faster-growing, defective oxide layers that crack and spall under the same conditions.
drafts.baseline: The Mn-containing CrFeCoNiMn alloy, which is expected to form an unstable oxide layer prone to cracking and spallation.
drafts.boundary: Applies to single-phase metallic solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloys under high-temperature (above 900 °C) exposure in defined oxidative or corrosive atmospheres; results may vary if multiphase microstructures or other environmental variables are introduced.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloy samples with X = Si, Mn, and Al. Expose these samples to a controlled oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for a series of thermal cycles. Monitor the oxide layer evolution using in-situ high-temperature microscopy and perform post-exposure evaluations using SEM, TEM, and XRD to analyze oxide morphology, thickness, composition, and adhesion.
measurements: Morphology and continuity of the oxide layer (via SEM/TEM)
Adhesion strength of the oxide to the substrate
Phase identification and lattice matching (via XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Si or Al containing alloys do not exhibit a notably more coherent and stable oxide layer compared to the Mn-containing alloy—in particular, if they display cracking or spallation rates similar to those of the Mn variant—the hypothesis that element-specific cation diffusion and lattice matching solely drive the formation of protective oxides is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the nature of the X element controls the stability of the protective oxide scale above 900 °C, such that when X is Al, a coherent, slow‐growing α-Al2O3 scale forms that adheres well to the underlying phase and minimizes cracking or spallation, whereas when X is Si or Mn the oxide products are less adherent or form noncoherent, rapidly growing layers prone to cracking. In addition, single-phase solid solution microstructures support a more uniform distribution of oxide-forming elements, reducing local stress concentrations at the oxide-metal interface compared to multiphase states.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) prepared either as a single-phase homogeneous solid solution or as a multiphase metallic structure.
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloys to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for prolonged periods.
drafts.conditions: High-temperature (≥900 °C) exposure in a controlled oxidizing/corrosive environment with a constant atmosphere; comparison between single-phase and multiphase microstructures.
drafts.structural_mediator: The coherence and uniformity of the oxide scale—specifically, the formation of a continuous, adherent α-Al2O3 layer in the Al-bearing alloy versus noncoherent or heterogeneous oxide layers when Si or Mn is used, and differences between single-phase and multiphase microstructures.
drafts.mechanism: Aluminum, due to its high oxygen affinity at high temperatures, forms a slow-growing and thermodynamically stable alumina (α-Al2O3) scale that limits oxygen ingress and reduces thermal stress mismatch at the interface. In contrast, Si and Mn yield oxides that are either less protective or more prone to growth stresses, promoting cracking or spallation. Uniform elemental distribution in a single-phase state further minimizes localized stress concentrations that can trigger oxide failure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Al, especially in a single-phase solid solution state, will develop a thin, uniform, and adherent oxide scale with parabolic (diffusion-controlled) kinetics, while alloys with X = Si or Mn, or multiphase microstructures, will exhibit thicker, nonuniform, or rapidly growing (or even spallation-prone) oxide scales.
drafts.baseline: Behavior of CrFeCoNi alloy lacking the specific oxide‐promoting element (i.e. without sufficient Al content) or with a multiphase microstructure known to produce less protective oxides.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to alloys operating above 900 °C in oxidizing or corrosive environments; results may differ at lower temperatures or with alternative atmospheres where different oxidation kinetics prevail.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX alloys with X systematically varied among Al, Si, and Mn, ensuring both single-phase and multiphase microstructures in separate samples. Subject all samples to an identical high-temperature (≥900 °C) oxidation or corrosive exposure in a controlled atmosphere for an extended duration. Characterize the oxide scale using SEM, XRD, and cross-sectional microscopy to assess thickness, uniformity, coherence, and evidence of cracking/spallation.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and growth rate (e.g., via weight gain measurements and microscopy)
Phase composition of the oxide layer (e.g., via XRD)
Oxide scale adhesion and presence of cracks/spallation (e.g., via SEM and cross-sectional imaging)
Comparative analysis between single-phase and multiphase alloy samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-bearing alloys (especially in the single-phase state) do not exhibit a thinner, coherent, slow-growing oxide scale in contrast to the Si- or Mn-bearing alloys, or if all alloy variants produce comparably adherent and continuous oxide layers regardless of X or microstructural state, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX HEAs, the nature of the fifth element (X) controls the type, growth rate, and mechanical coherence of the high-temperature oxide scale by modulating the balance between metal outward diffusion and oxygen inward diffusion. In particular, when X is Al, the alloy preferentially forms a slow-growing, coherent, and protective Al2O3 scale that resists cracking/spallation above 900 °C, whereas when X is Si or Mn, less protective mixed oxides form that are prone to rapid growth, high defect density, and eventual scale failure.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state (nominally equiatomic among Cr, Fe, Co, Ni and X where X = Si, Mn, or Al)
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloy to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C
drafts.conditions: High-temperature exposure (≥900 °C) in oxidizing (or corrosive) environments where oxygen (and/or additional aggressive species) are available; comparisons under identical thermal and environmental conditions
drafts.structural_mediator: The evolving surface oxide layer, particularly its composition (predominantly Al2O3 vs. mixed oxides), morphology (thin, coherent versus thick, strained, and cracked), and growth kinetics
drafts.mechanism: The addition of Al favors the formation of a thermodynamically stable, slow-growing Al2O3 with low oxygen and metal ion diffusivity, minimizing internal stresses and mismatch at the oxide/metal interface. In contrast, when the alloy contains Si or Mn, the resulting oxides (or mixed oxide phases) have higher growth rates and mechanical mismatches, resulting in cracking or spallation due to rapid diffusion and mismatch in thermal expansion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: For the Al-containing alloy, a thin, adherent, and slowly thickening layer of predominantly Al2O3 will form and remain coherent even after prolonged exposure above 900 °C. For the Si- or Mn-containing alloys, the surface oxide will be thicker, less uniform, containing mixed oxides, and will develop cracks and spallation over the same exposure period.
drafts.baseline: CrFeCoNiX alloys where X is either Si or Mn serve as the baseline (control) for comparison against the Al-containing variant.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys in either single- or multiphase solid solutions under high-temperature (≥900 °C) oxidative or corrosive environments; the observations are expected to hold under controlled laboratory exposure times representative of prolonged service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Al, Si, and Mn having identical processing histories and microstructures. Expose samples to an oxidizing atmosphere at 920 °C (above 900 °C) for a fixed duration (e.g., 100 hours). After exposure, characterize the oxide scales using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and cross-sectional analysis to determine oxide composition, thickness, and the presence/absence of cracking or spallation.
measurements: Adhesion and mechanical integrity tests (e.g., scratch or pull-off tests)
Mass gain measurements during oxidation kinetics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not exhibit a significantly more coherent, slow-growing, and protective oxide (dominated by Al2O3) compared to the Si- or Mn-containing alloys – or if any alloy with X = Si or Mn unexpectedly forms an oxide with similar protective features and minimal cracking – then the proposed mechanism linking the choice of X element with oxide stability at high temperatures is falsified.
